correctness.rationale: For |v|<b the uniformly inward tail drift gives an exponential Lyapunov function (choose its exponent below (b−|v|)/T); ellipticity and positive flipping give irreducibility. At v=0 the Gibbs density is comparable to a bilateral exponential, hence the reversible form has a gap on centered functions. In the weighted variables P/π and D/π the drift perturbation is B u=u′+(f/T)u, bounded H¹(π)→L²(π) and of mean zero; invert the diagonal operators on the normalized centered pair at fixed r and use a Neumann series for small v. The stationary law is in this space locally in v: at v=0 the positive-side tail exponents are 0, −b/T and (−b±√(b²+8rT))/(2T), simple for r>0; for small v both integrable exponents stay below −b/(2T), and the left tail is reflected. Thus the derivative D/v=−π(2r+K)⁻¹f/T is justified even with the cusps. Substitution into the specified full-state current gives the stated resolvent. The spectral measure for x has first moment T and second moment b², using Kx=−f weakly and |f|=b a.e. Positivity, strict monotonicity, strict concavity and analyticity follow from the positive spectral kernel; dominated convergence gives the two tails in the prescribed order. Subtracting the negative-half spill from the full shifted bilateral exponential gives the stated Gibbs variance; its derivative in a is positive. The Laplace transform of the continuous time covariance is exactly [V−T²χ(s/2)/s]/s. These calculations establish the full stated inverse claim.
residual_risks: The v-linearization holds at fixed positive r; it gives no uniform error estimate as r tends to zero or infinity.
No stability under noise or finite sampling is asserted.

originality.rationale: The same model and EPR identity are explicit prior work. A generic weak-force covariance transform is also an equilibrium fluctuation–response consequence: stationarity of σX gives Π=2rv⟨σX⟩/T, and convolution of −C′/T with exp(−2rt) produces the response formula. These are not freestanding novel principles. What survives is the exact use of the rate curve to identify both cusp parameters, via different low- and high-frequency spectral moments and a strictly invertible equilibrium variance, together with its covariance interpretation in this model. The closest inspected exact same-model formulas do not give this inverse identification.

value.rationale: In the already studied cusp model, the rate scan extracts the confinement slope and then the well separation from different ends of one observable, without reconstructing or fitting the full stationary density or assuming a finite-mode spectrum. The exact covariance interpretation explains the low-rate calibration and identifies the information content of the full curve. This is a concrete motivated inverse result, not novelty of the equilibrium fluctuation–response principle.
residual_risks: Uniqueness requires exact response data and known T; analytic extension and tail extrapolation are not necessarily numerically well conditioned.
